newsitem.title: USA: Corruption fight moves to fore in IMF-Kenya row.
newsitem.headline: Corruption fight moves to fore in IMF-Kenya row.

text.p: Delays and procrastination in Kenya's crackdown against graft were behind an International Monetary Fund decision to halt lending, but analysts said on Friday the IMF fight against corruption was here to stay.

The decision, which sent shock waves through financial markets in Nairobi, was the strongest and bluntest example of new IMF thinking that good, honest, open government is an essential part of economic reform.

"You have seen increased emphasis on good governance at the IMF and the World Bank in the last year or two and this is probably a case where their credibility was at stake," said Morris Goldstein, senior fellow at the Institute for International Economics. "It seems to be a glaring example."

Goldstein, who used to work for the IMF, said he expected to see more stress in future on good governance, encompassing issues ranging from poor organisation, wasted cash or inefficiency to official corruption.

Corruption, while not mentioned explicitly by the IMF, was high on the fund's radar screen on Thursday when it halted a three-year loan to Kenya and said the government's response to a July 24 deadline had been inadequate.

That was the latest of several ultimatums extended by the IMF, which was increasingly worried that the Kenyan government was not acting decisively to root out corruption and increase public sector accountability and transparency.
After the IMF's action, Kenyan Attorney-General Amos Wako on Friday published a tough anti-corruption draft bill.
One notorious example of corruption in Kenya was the 1992 Goldenberg scandal, in which a company was paid $100 million under an official export compensation scheme for gold and diamonds.
Kenya, a major producer of commodities like coffee, has no diamond deposits and produces little gold.

"The management of the IMF has examined Kenya's request for an extension of the current (loan) and considers that the measures that the government is prepared to take fall short of meeting the clearly-expressed concerns of IMF member countries in the area of governance," an IMF spokesman said, using surprisingly tough and undiplomatic language.
One analyst, who asked not to be named, said it appeared to be the first time that the IMF had linked payments on a loan to government actions so directly.
"I can remember several stand-offs with various IMF members, but this is the first time where the issue of governance has been discussed quite so openly," he said.
The stress on "good governance" has become more and more pronounced at the IMF and the World Bank.
A major World Bank report released last month said that good government, based on sound laws and a stable economy, was an essential precondition for economic growth.
"The message is not big government or small government, but that an effective state is vital for development," World Bank official Ajay Chhibber said when the report was released.
The bank tracks whether its funds are used in a corrupt way, but it has not so far made lending conditional on such things as a country meeting criteria on official corruption.
